description: Sources of contamination, the five food-poisoning bacteria and general symptoms of food poisoning.
content_html:
How Bacteria Get into Food

Bacterial contamination rarely arrives in one dramatic moment — it usually creeps in through a series of small mistakes. A chopping board used for raw chicken that is then used for salad leaves, a food handler who forgets to wash their hands after visiting the toilet, a pet walking across a kitchen surface — these are the real routes by which harmful bacteria reach the food we eat. Understanding the sources of bacterial contamination is the first step in preventing it.

The main sources of contamination are:

  • Other contaminated foods — particularly raw foods: Raw meat, poultry, eggs, seafood and unwashed vegetables all carry bacteria naturally. Raw chicken is one of the most significant sources of campylobacter in the UK. Even raw vegetables from the soil can carry bacteria such as e-coli if they have been in contact with animal manure during growing or harvesting.
  • Work surfaces and equipment: Bacteria survive on worktops, chopping boards, knives and mixing bowls for hours. A surface that was used for raw fish and wiped down with a damp cloth (rather than washed with hot soapy water) remains a contamination risk.
  • The people cooking: Hands are the main vector from person to food. Poor personal hygiene — sneezing over open food, touching the face, failing to wash hands after handling raw meat — is a leading cause of staphylococcus aureus contamination specifically.
  • Pests: Mice, rats, cockroaches and flies carry bacteria on their bodies and in their droppings. A fly landing on cooked food and then on raw meat transfers bacteria in both directions.
  • Waste food and rubbish: Decomposing food in bins creates a reservoir of bacteria that can spread if bins are stored near food preparation areas or if hands are not washed after handling waste.
Key Fact

The five sources of bacterial contamination are: other contaminated foods (especially raw meat, poultry, eggs, seafood and vegetables); work surfaces and equipment; the people cooking; pests; and waste food and rubbish.

The Five Food-Poisoning Bacteria

You need to know five specific bacteria by name — their typical sources, the conditions that favour them and the key control methods. A short-answer question asking you to name two and give their sources is very common. Memorise all five: campylobacter, e-coli, salmonella, listeria and staphylococcus aureus. Students who know only salmonella consistently lose marks on this topic.

Campylobacter is found primarily in raw and undercooked poultry, particularly chicken. It is also found in unpasteurised milk, contaminated water and the intestines of farm animals. It is responsible for the majority of bacterial food poisoning cases in the UK each year. The key control is thorough cooking — campylobacter is destroyed when poultry reaches an internal temperature of 75°C throughout. Do not wash raw chicken: washing spreads campylobacter-laden droplets up to a metre around the sink. Campylobacter does not multiply particularly fast in food at room temperature; its main risk is survival from undercooking.

E-coli (Escherichia coli): Most strains of e-coli are harmless gut bacteria, but certain strains (particularly E. coli O157) produce toxins that cause severe illness. Sources include undercooked ground beef (minced meat), contaminated water, and raw vegetables grown in soil fertilised with animal manure. Control methods: thorough cooking of minced meat to 75°C throughout; washing raw vegetables; good hand hygiene; pasteurising milk.

Salmonella: Found in raw poultry, raw eggs, raw meat and some unpasteurised dairy products. Contamination can come from the inside of an egg if the laying hen was infected, which is why runny fried eggs carry a risk if the eggs are not from a Lion Code flock. Control: thorough cooking to 75°C; good personal hygiene when handling raw eggs; refrigerating raw poultry separately from cooked foods.

Listeria (Listeria monocytogenes) is unusual because it can multiply at refrigerator temperatures — between 0°C and 5°C — making it a particular threat in chilled ready-to-eat foods. Sources include soft mould-ripened cheeses (such as Brie and Camembert), pâté, cold deli meats and smoked fish. Listeria is especially dangerous for pregnant women, where it can cause miscarriage or serious illness in the newborn. Control: keep chilled food below 5°C and consume within use-by date; vulnerable groups should avoid high-risk products.

Staphylococcus aureus is carried naturally on human skin, in the nose, throat and hair. It reaches food when food handlers sneeze, cough, touch their face or have skin infections such as cuts or boils. Once in the food, it multiplies and produces toxins that are heat-resistant — meaning cooking the food again will not destroy the toxin even if the bacteria are killed. High-risk situations include cooked rice, egg mayonnaise, and cream-filled pastries left at room temperature. Control: strict personal hygiene; keeping food below 5°C or above 63°C; covering cuts with blue waterproof plasters.

Key Fact

The five food-poisoning bacteria you must know: campylobacter (raw poultry), e-coli (undercooked minced beef, contaminated water), salmonella (raw poultry, raw eggs), listeria (soft cheeses, chilled ready-to-eat meats — can grow at fridge temperature), staphylococcus aureus (human skin/nose/throat, cooked foods at room temperature).

Symptoms of Food Poisoning

Food poisoning is caused either by the bacteria themselves infecting the gut, or by toxins they have already produced in the food before it is eaten. The general symptoms are consistent across most types, although their severity and timing vary:

  • Nausea (feeling sick)
  • Vomiting
  • Diarrhoea
  • Stomach cramps and abdominal pain
  • Fever (raised body temperature)
  • Headache and general malaise

Symptoms typically develop between one hour and several days after eating contaminated food, depending on the bacterium. Staphylococcus aureus toxin can cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 8 hours (often 1 to 6 hours) because the toxin is already present in the food. Campylobacter infections typically take two to five days to develop because the bacteria must first establish in the gut. Most healthy adults recover within a few days, but young children, elderly people, pregnant women and those with weakened immune systems can develop serious complications, including dehydration and, in rare cases, kidney failure.
exam_tip_html: A frequent mistake on 3-mark Describe or 4-mark Explain questions about food-poisoning bacteria is naming only salmonella. The specification lists five bacteria — campylobacter, e-coli, salmonella, listeria and staphylococcus aureus — and examiners write questions that test all of them. If the question asks you to “name two food-poisoning bacteria and give one source for each”, choosing the two you can explain fully is better than guessing at names you cannot support with a source. Listeria is the one students most often forget: remember it by its unusual ability to grow at fridge temperature and its particular risk to pregnant women. Staphylococcus aureus is notable because its toxins are heat-resistant — reheating contaminated food does not make it safe. These two distinguishing features are high-tariff details that regularly separate Secure from Mastering answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bacterial contamination reaches food from five main sources: other raw foods, work surfaces and equipment, the people cooking, pests, and waste food and rubbish.
  • The five food-poisoning bacteria are campylobacter, e-coli, salmonella, listeria and staphylococcus aureus — each with distinct sources and control methods.
  • Listeria can grow at fridge temperature; staphylococcus aureus produces heat-resistant toxins — these are the two most distinguishing features that separate them from the others.

practice_questions.text:
Which food-poisoning bacterium can grow at refrigerator temperatures and is especially dangerous for pregnant women?
A. Campylobacter
B. Salmonella
C. Listeria
D. Staphylococcus aureus
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C (Listeria). Campylobacter and salmonella are destroyed by thorough cooking and do not grow well at fridge temperatures. Staphylococcus aureus produces heat-resistant toxins but does not grow well at fridge temperatures.

practice_questions.text: Name two food-poisoning bacteria and give one typical source for each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct bacterium-source pair, up to 2 marks. Accept any two from: campylobacter — raw/undercooked poultry; e-coli — undercooked minced beef or contaminated water or raw vegetables; salmonella — raw poultry or raw eggs; listeria — soft mould-ripened cheeses, cold deli meats, smoked fish; staphylococcus aureus — food handlers' skin/nose/throat or cooked foods at room temperature. The bacterium and source must be correctly matched for the mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe three symptoms of bacterial food poisoning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly described symptom, up to 3 marks. Accept: nausea; vomiting; diarrhoea; stomach cramps/abdominal pain; fever/raised temperature; headache; general malaise. Answers must describe the symptom, not just name it — e.g. 'raised body temperature' is better than just 'fever' but both are acceptable for 1 mark each.

practice_questions.text: Omar is a food handler at a school canteen. He has a small cut on his finger and has been preparing egg mayonnaise sandwiches. Explain why this situation poses a food safety risk and how Omar should address it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the specific risk (staphylococcus aureus on skin/in wounds); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (bacteria transfers from cut to food during handling); 1 mark for correct control method (cover cut with a blue waterproof plaster); 1 mark for a second linked explanation or additional control (wash hands thoroughly before handling food; egg mayonnaise is a high-risk chilled food that must be kept below 5°C to slow bacterial growth). Must use linking language ('because' or 'this means that') for the explanation marks.

practice_questions.text: Assess the food safety risks associated with preparing and serving a chicken dish at a community cookery event. In your answer, refer to sources of contamination, the bacteria involved, and how the risks can be controlled.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Thorough analysis breaking the preparation and serving process into distinct stages: buying/storage (campylobacter on raw chicken; refrigerate at 0–5°C; keep separate from ready-to-eat foods); preparation (cross-contamination from board/knife to other foods; wash hands; use separate colour-coded boards); cooking (must reach 75°C throughout to destroy campylobacter and salmonella; use a temperature probe); serving and holding (keep above 63°C or below 5°C; time in danger zone; staphylococcus aureus risk if food handlers have skin infections). Names at least three bacteria with their specific sources and controls. Examines consequences (not just lists risks) — e.g. links campylobacter survival to undercooking, links staphylococcus aureus toxin heat-stability to the importance of preventing contamination in the first place. Sustained application to the community event context throughout.

Secure (5–7 marks): Most stages of the process addressed; at least two bacteria named with sources; controls given but some links between risk and consequence are missing. Context applied but not consistently.

Developing (3–4 marks): Some relevant risks identified; one or two bacteria named; controls listed without full explanation of why they work. Limited application to the event context.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic food safety points (cook thoroughly, wash hands) with little or no bacterium-specific knowledge or reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Identify the food-poisoning bacterium whose toxins remain dangerous even after the contaminated food is reheated.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for staphylococcus aureus. Accept 'staph aureus' or 'S. aureus' but not just 'staph' without the genus context.

knowledge_checks.q: Which bacterium is primarily associated with raw and undercooked poultry and is the most common cause of bacterial food poisoning in the UK?
Which of the following is NOT one of the five food-poisoning bacteria listed in the specification?
Staphylococcus aureus is dangerous because it produces heat-resistant _____, which are not destroyed by cooking the food again.
Unlike most food-poisoning bacteria, listeria can multiply at temperatures as low as 0°C, meaning it can grow inside a _____.
Match each food-poisoning bacterium to its most characteristic source or feature.
right: Raw poultry — destroyed by cooking to 75°C
Human skin, nose and throat — toxins are heat-resistant
Raw eggs and raw poultry — also found in unpasteurised dairy

flashcard_questions.q: Name all five food-poisoning bacteria on the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Campylobacter, e-coli, salmonella, listeria, staphylococcus aureus — all five must be known.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the primary food source associated with campylobacter?
What unusual property makes listeria especially dangerous in chilled ready-to-eat foods?
flashcard_questions.a: It can multiply at refrigerator temperatures (0–5°C), unlike most food-poisoning bacteria.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is staphylococcus aureus still dangerous even after contaminated food is reheated?
flashcard_questions.a: Its toxins are heat-resistant and are not destroyed by cooking.

flashcard_questions.q: How does staphylococcus aureus typically reach food?
flashcard_questions.a: Via food handlers' skin, nose, throat or infected cuts and wounds.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main source of e-coli O157 in food?
flashcard_questions.a: Undercooked minced beef and contaminated water or unwashed vegetables.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two foods associated with listeria contamination.
flashcard_questions.a: Soft mould-ripened cheese (e.g. Brie) and cold deli meats.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should you never wash raw chicken?
flashcard_questions.a: Washing spreads campylobacter droplets across the sink and nearby surfaces.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two vulnerable groups particularly at risk from listeria infection.
flashcard_questions.a: Pregnant women and elderly people (also immunocompromised people).

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five main sources of bacterial contamination in food preparation.
flashcard_questions.a: Contaminated raw foods; work surfaces/equipment; people cooking; pests; waste/rubbish.

flashcard_questions.q: What general symptom distinguishes a fever from nausea in a food-poisoning episode?
flashcard_questions.a: A fever is a raised body temperature; nausea is the feeling of sickness before vomiting.

flashcard_questions.q: Which of the five food-poisoning bacteria is associated with raw eggs?

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which harmful bacteria are transferred to food from another source, making the food unsafe to eat.
A bacterium found mainly in raw poultry and a leading cause of food poisoning in the UK, destroyed by thorough cooking.
A bacterium that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (as low as 0°C) and is particularly dangerous for pregnant women, elderly people and those with a weakened immune system.
A bacterium carried on human skin and in the nose and throat that produces heat-resistant toxins in high-protein cooked foods left at room temperature.
